title: Coles profit hit by underpayment scandal
excerpt: Coles chief executive Leah Weckert said it had been another consistent set of results for the supermarket that had been through multiple court proceedings.
body:
Coles reported its full-year results this week, with profit weighed down by the cost of the underpayment scandal that has been winding through the courts. Chief executive Leah Weckert said it had been 'another consistent set of results' for the supermarket, with the wage-recovery costs now a permanent feature of the P&L.

Our take: this is the latest in a string of large-employer underpayment scandals. Woolworths, Bunnings, Caltex, 7-Eleven, George Calombaris's Made Establishment, and now Coles. The pattern is clear: these are not isolated payroll mistakes, they are systematic failures of large-employer payroll systems that have been running on bad award interpretation for years. The Fair Work Ombudsman has been stepping up prosecutions, and the penalties now include back-pay of up to ten years, plus fines. For workers, the upside is that the regulator is finally catching up. For investors, the underpayment cost is a permanent line item, not a one-off, and it deserves to be capitalised into every large-employer valuation.

The most under-reported detail: most of the underpaid workers were casual or part-time, paid at base award rates but missing penalty rates, weekend rates, or public-holiday rates. If you work in retail, hospitality, or fast food, and you have not checked your payslips against the award in the last twelve months, do it now.
whatItMeans: If you work in retail, hospitality, or fast food: Check your payslips against the relevant award using the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator. The FWO can back-pay up to ten years for award breaches, and up to six years for contract breaches.
If you are a Coles or Woolworths shareholder: Underpayment costs are now structural, not one-off. Adjust your valuation model accordingly.
If you are a hiring manager at a large employer: Treat payroll as a compliance risk, not an HR function. The cost of getting it wrong now exceeds the cost of an audit.
If you think you have been underpaid in the past: The FWO complaints process is free. The window to claim goes back further than most people realise.
